Mathematical biology

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 24k Articles: 460
Mathematical biology uses mathematical models to connect biological mechanisms with quantitative predictions. Differential equations can track changing quantities, while population dynamics, enzyme kinetics and gene regulatory networks ask how growth, reactions and feedback shape living systems. A useful mathematical model states its assumptions and units: a simple chemostat, for example, reveals how nutrient supply and removal jointly determine whether a culture persists.

Leslie-Gower predator-prey model

Words: 135 Articles: 1
Mathematical biology OurBigBook.com
The system u˙=u(1−u)−auv/(u+d), v˙=bv(1−v/u) combines logistic prey growth, saturating predation and a predator carrying level proportional to prey density. Its unique positive equilibrium is u=v=s, where (1−s)(s+d)=as. Its Jacobian matrix has determinant bs(1−a−d)2+4d​/(s+d)>0 and trace s(1−d−2s)/(s+d)−b. The positive trapping construction for the Leslie-Gower model gives a compact positive region and a limit cycle whenever this equilibrium is a repeller.

Positive trapping construction for the Leslie-Gower model (P=ue−v)

Words: 82
Leslie-Gower predator-prey model OurBigBook.com
A rectangular upper bound u,v≤M, M>1, is inward pointing for the Leslie-Gower predator-prey model. To avoid the singular edge u=0, use P=ue−v and the inequality P˙/P≥1−u[1+(a/d+b)2/(4b)], obtained by completing a square. Choose εeM sufficiently small and 0<η<ε. Then u≤M, η≤v≤M, P≥ε is a compact forward-invariant set in the positive quadrant. Removing an outward-flow neighborhood of a repelling equilibrium leaves a trapping region without equilibria, so the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem yields a periodic omega-limit orbit.

Competition model

Words: 60
Mathematical biology OurBigBook.com
In a biological competition model, increasing one population reduces the growth of another. A two-species example is u˙=ru(1−u−v), v˙=v(1−βu), with both cross-effects negative. This asymmetric example has self-limitation only in u; disappearance of u therefore permits unbounded growth of v. For s≪Ks​, μ(s)≈(μmax​/Ks​)s; for s≫Ks​, μ(s) approaches μmax​. Its derivative μ′(s)=μmax​Ks​/(Ks​+s)2 is positive: more nutrient increases the specific growth rate, with progressively smaller increments.
For example, take μmax​=1h−1 and Ks​=1gL−1. Nutrient concentrations of 0, 1 and 9gL−1 give specific growth rates 0, 0.5 and 0.9h−1. The Monod equation is useful because two measurable parameters describe both nutrient scarcity and saturation. It assumes the other conditions affecting growth remain controlled and does not represent inhibition at high nutrient concentration. Although its formula resembles the Michaelis-Menten equation, a whole culture's specific growth rate combines many processes; the resemblance alone does not derive it from Michaelis-Menten kinetics or identify Ks​ with a Michaelis constant.
In his 1949 review, Monod presents the hyperbolic rate law as an empirical fit in equation (2), pp. 383-384, and discusses the difficulty of identifying a single growth-controlling reaction. His reported division rates use doublings per unit time; the natural-exponential specific growth rate used here is that division rate multiplied by ln2. [ref].

A chemostat maintains a well-mixed culture at constant volume V by feeding fresh nutrient solution and removing culture at the same volumetric flow Q. Its dilution rate is D=Q/V. Mixing makes the outflow's nutrient concentration and biomass concentration equal to those inside the vessel; continuous replacement supplies nutrient and also removes growing cells.
The simplest one-nutrient chemostat uses nutrient concentration s(t), biomass concentration x(t), constant feed nutrient concentration sin​>0, and constant biomass yield Y>0. Assume a cell-free feed, one growth-limiting nutrient, constant volume, and no cell retention, death or additional nutrient consumption for maintenance. With specific growth rate μ(s), its ordinary differential equations are
dtds​=D(sin​−s)−Yμ(s)x​,dtdx​=(μ(s)−D)x.
(3)
The nutrient balance contains inflow Dsin​, outflow Ds, and consumption μ(s)x/Y; the biomass balance contains production μ(s)x and removal Dx. If s is in grams of nutrient per litre and x in grams of dry biomass per litre, Y is grams of dry biomass produced per gram of nutrient consumed. Thus both balances have units of their respective concentration per time. The Monod equation supplies an empirical choice of μ(s); the balances themselves express the stated production, consumption and transport assumptions.
The appeal of a chemostat is that, at a positive chemostat steady state, adjusting the pump sets the specific growth rate to D. The residual nutrient concentration then adjusts to that rate, and the available nutrient together with biomass yield sets the biomass concentration. This gives a controlled way to compare cultures at selected growth rates and a simple quantitative warning of chemostat washout.
Two 1950 publications on continuous culture are Novick and Szilard's Description of the Chemostat, Science 112(2920), 715-716, dated 15 December, and Monod's La technique de culture continue. Théorie et applications, Annales de l'Institut Pasteur 79, 390-410. The latter's original bibliographic details are reproduced in the contents of Monod's collected papers. These references identify contemporary publications without establishing priority between them. [ref]. [ref].

Chemostat washout means the culture's biomass concentration tends to zero because growth cannot sustain replacement of the cells leaving the vessel. In the ideal Monod equation chemostat with D>0, its equilibrium is (s,x)=(sin​,0). Its Jacobian matrix has eigenvalues −D and μ(sin​)−D: a small inoculum grows when D<μ(sin​), whereas chemostat washout is locally asymptotically stable when D>μ(sin​). For nonnegative initial concentrations, chemostat washout occurs for D≥μ(sin​); the boundary case also loses biomass asymptotically.
At D=Dc​ the positive chemostat steady state meets the chemostat washout equilibrium, and one eigenvalue is zero, so linearization alone does not decide the boundary case. On the invariant nutrient-equivalent balance s+x/Y=sin​, small positive x obeys x˙=−[μ′(sin​)/Y]x2+O(x3): nutrient consumption lowers the specific growth rate below Dc​, leading to slow decay rather than a positive biomass concentration. Density dependence

Words: 135 Articles: 1
Population dynamics OurBigBook.com
A population model has density dependence when its per-capita recruitment, survival or growth depends on population abundance relative to habitat or resource scale. Negative density dependence reduces per-capita growth as crowding increases. In a discrete-generation model, a strong enough decline can make the next total population decrease as the present total increases, producing overcompensation and possible alternating generations. The ecological mechanism and the mathematical stability calculation should be distinguished.

Overcompensation occurs when a larger present population produces a smaller total population in the next generation over part of the relevant range. It is stronger than a decline of per-capita growth alone. For F(u)=αu/(β+uγ) with γ>1, the large-abundance response F(u)∼αu1−γ decreases with abundance. Stronger feedback can drive a fixed-point multiplier through minus one, but that local threshold alone does not establish chaotic behaviour.

Population dynamics OurBigBook.com
A carrying capacity is an abundance scale at which a specified environment's net population growth vanishes. In the logistic growth equation, positive unharvested populations approach K. It depends on the species, resources and environment rather than being an immutable universal population limit.
The useful distinction is between a growth rate and a sustainable abundance. In a logistic differential equation, r controls how quickly a population responds, while the carrying capacity K sets the positive equilibrium point. Increasing r with K fixed accelerates approach without raising that equilibrium. Increasing K changes the destination. The logistic differential equation diagrams show populations approaching the same carrying capacity from below and above.
In ecological use, the carrying capacity describes what a particular environment can support under specified conditions. Nutrient supply, available space, and accumulated waste can change those conditions; it is not a permanent property of a species alone. A population temporarily above a carrying capacity is possible. In the simplest constant-K logistic growth equation, its net growth becomes negative; real population dynamics can include delays, seasonal variation, and changing resources that the basic mathematical model omits. Compartmental models (epidemiology) OurBigBook.com
This generation-based compartmental model replenishes the susceptible compartment by B>0 per step and transfers αSt​It​ individuals into the next infectious generation. Members of the current infectious compartment leave it after one step. In scaled variables x=αS, y=αI, r=αB, the update is x′=x+r−xy, y′=xy.
Its only fixed point is (S∗​,I∗​)=(1/α,B). There is no finite disease-free fixed point, since susceptible recruitment continues when I=0. The Jacobian matrix at the fixed point is M=(1−rr​−11​), with determinant one and trace 2−r. For 0<r<4, its two distinct eigenvalues have modulus one, so the linearized iterates are bounded and oscillatory. At r=4, the repeated eigenvalue −1 has a nontrivial Jordan block, making generic linearized iterates grow linearly. For r>4, one eigenvalue has modulus greater than one.
Thus 0<r<4 gives neutral linear stability, not asymptotic stability. Unit-modulus multipliers do not determine nonlinear stability. Recruitment can restore susceptibility above 1/α after a wave, allowing repeated infection growth; a closed SIR model without replenishment has a different susceptible balance.

For frequency-dependent transmission with homogeneous mixing, each member of the susceptible compartment experiences force of infection λ=βI/N=βi. Consequently the total flow into the infectious compartment is βSI/N people per unit time. The constant β combines the contact frequency and the chance that a relevant contact causes infection, and has units of inverse time. Holding the infectious compartment's fraction fixed holds each person's force of infection fixed when N changes. An unnormalized mass-action infection convention instead writes the total flow as bSI, where b=β/N has units of inverse person-time; these two coefficients must not be confused.

SIR model (s+i+r=1)

Words: 2k Articles: 21
Compartmental models (epidemiology) OurBigBook.com
The SIR model is a mathematical model of an epidemic that follows three groups: a susceptible compartment whose members can acquire infection, an infectious compartment whose members can pass it on, and a removed compartment whose members neither acquire nor pass on infection. The letters stand for susceptible, infectious and recovered or removed. Here we study the simplest closed, constant-parameter version, with homogeneous mixing and no births, deaths, migration or waning immunity. A person who leaves the infectious compartment never returns to the susceptible compartment in this version.[ref]
The appeal of the SIR model is that one can explain a rise and fall in the infectious compartment without changing anyone's behavior: fewer opportunities for new infection eventually reverse the growth. The SIR first integral even determines the SIR infection peak without computing its time. These are useful deductions from explicit assumptions. The stipulated numbers below illustrate the mathematical model; they are neither estimates for an actual disease nor a forecast or medical advice.
Kermack and McKendrick's 1927 paper, "A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics", in Proceedings of the Royal Society A, is an early foundation for the SIR model. Its DOI is 10.1098/rspa.1927.0118, also recorded in the Royal Society's archive of contemporary referee reports.[ref][ref]

SIR model OurBigBook.com
The removed compartment consists of people permanently excluded from both acquiring and passing on infection in the SIR model. Its count is R(t) and its fraction is r(t)=R(t)/N. In a variant that counts deaths within R, conservation of population would concern the original cohort, rather than the number currently alive.[ref]

For frequency-dependent transmission, the closed SIR model is a system of ordinary differential equations for the fractions s,i,r:
dtds​=−βsi,dtdi​=βsi−γi,dtdr​=γi,s+i+r=1.
(38)

With a constant recovery rate, the associated individual time in the infectious compartment has an exponential distribution with mean 1/γ; the SIR model does not require every person to spend exactly that long there. The fractions themselves have no units.[ref]
For counts S=Ns, I=Ni, R=Nr, the same SIR model equations read
dtdS​=−βNSI​,dtdI​=βNSI​−γI,dtdR​=γI,S+I+R=N.
(39)
The factor 1/N keeps the same β in both descriptions. Dropping it while keeping these units would fail dimensional analysis. Some existing SIR model variants use the unnormalized mass-action infection convention instead, including the SIR susceptible-recovered identity; their coefficient is b=β/N in the notation used here.
Adding the SIR model equations gives d(s+i+r)/dt=0, a short proof of conservation of population. Nonnegative starting fractions stay nonnegative: the outflow from either the susceptible compartment or the infectious compartment vanishes when that group is empty, while dr/dt≥0. Thus the susceptible compartment can only shrink and the removed compartment can only grow.
For a concrete initial value problem, stipulate
β=0.3day−1,γ=0.1day−1,(s0​,i0​,r0​)=(0.99,0.01,0).
(40)
At the start, the flow into the infectious compartment is 0.3×0.99×0.01=0.00297 of the total per day, and the flow into the removed compartment is 0.1×0.01=0.00100 of the total per day. Hence di/dt=0.00197 per day. If N=1000, these correspond to model rates of 2.97 and 1.00 people per day, and net growth 1.97 people per day. A rate need not be an integer count of events on any particular day.
For this SIR model, the basic reproduction number is
R0​=γβ​=3.
(41)
It describes one introduced member of the infectious compartment in an otherwise wholly susceptible compartment. The instantaneous reproduction number at the actual starting state is R0​s0​=2.97, obtained by freezing the current conditions and the current susceptible compartment's fraction. More generally it is R0​s(t) in this SIR model. The basic reproduction number is a ratio of two rates, so it has no units; r0​ is a different quantity, the initial removed compartment's fraction.
While i>0, its instantaneous relative growth is

Initially this equals 0.3×0.99−0.1=0.197day−1. Freezing s≈s0​ gives the early exponential growth approximation i(t)≈0.01e0.197t with t measured in days. It must fail as the susceptible compartment shrinks. An epidemic invasion threshold occurs at R0​s0​=1; if i0​=0, the deterministic SIR model stays at i=0 even above that threshold.

SIRS Markov chain OurBigBook.com
For convergent initial proportions, the scaled SIRS Markov chain converges uniformly in probability on each fixed finite interval to the solution of these equations. The Poisson time-change representation of a Markov chain writes it as its integrated drift plus centered Poisson errors. Bounded rates, Poisson concentration and the Gronwall inequality control the error. This finite-time limit does not by itself justify an approximation over time intervals growing with the population size.

The high-wavenumber positive term is diffusive smoothing; the negative chemotactic term drives aggregation.

Chemoattractant

Chemotaxis OurBigBook.com
A chemoattractant is a substance whose spatial distribution can bias responsive biological cells to migrate towards higher concentration. A directional response to its gradient is chemotaxis; a change only in movement speed does not by itself establish a directional response.

Words: 51
Chemotaxis OurBigBook.com
Temporal sensing in bacterial chemotaxis compares changing stimulation during movement with a recent adapted baseline. Attractant increases can lengthen runs and decreases can increase tumbling, producing biased movement up a chemical gradient. Rapid spatially uniform concentration steps distinguish a temporal response from a requirement for front-to-back spatial comparison.[ref]

The trace is negative, so an instability requires Q(q)<0. Without a cutoff, the sharp continuous-wavenumber threshold is B>2DAγ​. With q>q0​, minimize Dq+Aγ/q over that range; its unconstrained minimizer is Aγ/D​. Discrete geometries additionally require an actual allowed Laplacian eigenvalue in the open unstable band.

Biopolymer mechanics studies bending, stretching, thermal fluctuations, and force-induced deformation of filamentous biological macromolecules.

Helix-coil transition model

Words: 284 Articles: 2
Biopolymer mechanics OurBigBook.com
A helix-coil transition model assigns local states of a biopolymer to an ordered helical conformation or a disordered coil conformation. Their competing free energies determine the tendency to form a helix, while the cost of boundaries between regions gives cooperativity: forming a new helical run can be less favorable than extending an existing one. A coil state is a class of disordered conformations, not a claim that the whole molecule is an ideal chain. The Zimm-Bragg model is a simple nearest-neighbour statistical model of this competition.

A homogeneous DNA zipper permitting exactly one contiguous paired block of length j≥1 has N−j+1 block positions and weight κsj−1. Consequently its partition function is q=κ∑j=1N​(N−j+1)sj−1=κ[sN+1−(N+1)s+N]/(s−1)2. The removable value at s=1 is κN(N+1)/2. At large s, q∼κsN−1. Including an unpaired state gives the full partition function 1+q; the large-s limit is not uniform in arbitrarily small initiation weight.

A polymerization Brownian ratchet advances a filament by incorporating a monomer when thermal motion opens enough space between its tip and a resisting load. The irreversible chemical step rectifies the load's fluctuations. The elementary load advance a depends on tip geometry; two staggered strands can give a=δ/2, whereas two aligned strands do not automatically give this step. An effective addition rate must refer to the same elementary advance.

Ideal chain

Words: 1k Articles: 15
Biopolymer mechanics OurBigBook.com
An ideal chain, also called a freely jointed chain, consists of fixed-length links with independent orientations and no bending energy between successive links. It neglects segment interactions and excluded volume. A one-dimensional freely jointed chain restricts each link to two orientations. At fixed force its canonical partition function factors into one-link angular integrals. The resulting extension is entropic and depends on temperature and on whether the orientations are allowed in one, two, or three dimensions.

Extensible freely jointed chain (z=LL(fb/(kB​T))+Lf/S)

Words: 51
Ideal chain OurBigBook.com
A freely jointed chain supplemented with axial segment compliance. A simple phenomenological additive law is z=LL(fb/(kB​T))+Lf/S, where L=Nb, L is the Langevin function and S is an axial stretch modulus with units of force. This adds energetic compliance to the entropic spring; it is not an exact angular average for arbitrary harmonic-link statistics.

Freely rotating chain

Words: 194 Articles: 2
Ideal chain OurBigBook.com
A freely rotating chain has fixed bond length and fixed angle between successive forward bond vectors, with independently uniform torsion angles. It neglects interactions between distant chain segments. The fixed angle introduces short-range orientational correlations even though the torsional rotations are unrestricted. Its characteristic ratio of a freely rotating chain converts those correlations into an end-to-end size; its equivalent long-chain link is the Kuhn length of a freely rotating chain.

A lipid assembly containing a bilayer-like region whose edges are stabilized by other components, often short-chain lipids or detergents. Size and composition affect its use as a membrane mimic.

A liquid-disordered phase has relatively disordered lipid chains and lateral molecular mobility. Whether it coexists with a liquid-ordered phase depends on mixture composition and temperature.

A liquid-ordered phase combines relatively ordered lipid chains with lateral molecular mobility. It is distinct from a solid gel and can coexist with a liquid-disordered phase in suitable mixtures.

spontaneous curvature is the preferred curvature of a membrane or monolayer in a specified elastic description. Headgroup hydration, chain geometry and leaflet composition can change it; the sign depends on the chosen surface-normal convention.

Lipid bilayer nanodisc

Lipid bilayer OurBigBook.com
A lipid bilayer nanodisc is a small bilayer patch stabilized at its edge, often by a surrounding scaffold. It permits controlled lipid composition and study of membrane-associated proteins, while lacking the two separately sealed aqueous compartments of a closed lipid vesicle.

Uniqueness of the packed spherical bilayer radius (R3−r3=3(v/a)(R2+r2))

Words: 86
Lipid bilayer OurBigBook.com
In an incompressible, noninterdigitating lipid bilayer with negligible head-group thickness, let the inner radius be r>0, molecular tail volume v>0 and head-group area a>0. Counting heads on both membrane leaflets and conserving tail volume gives R3−r3=3(v/a)(R2+r2). For R>r, the function q(R)=(R3−r3)/(R2+r2) has derivative (R4+3R2r2+2Rr3)/(R2+r2)2>0, starts at zero and tends to infinity. Thus exactly one candidate outer radius exists in this geometric model. A maximum tail length l additionally requires rm​−r≤l and R−rm​≤l, where rm3​=r3+3(v/a)r2. Uniqueness does not establish compatibility with arbitrary molecular lengths.

Membrane leaflet

Words: 31
Lipid bilayer OurBigBook.com
A membrane leaflet is one of the two layers forming a lipid bilayer. In a phospholipid-based cell membrane, the hydrophilic regions face the adjacent water, and the hydrophobic regions face the interior shared by the two membrane leaflets.

Line tension (γ)

Words: 155 Articles: 2
Lipid bilayer OurBigBook.com
Line tension is energy per unit length of a boundary, such as the edge between two phases of a lipid bilayer. Positive line tension tends to minimize the perimeter at fixed domain area. Its dimensions and geometry differ from surface tension, which is energy per unit area.

Fixed-area capillary spectrum of a circular boundary (⟨um2​⟩)

Words: 114 Articles: 1
Line tension OurBigBook.com
For a circular domain of radius R0​ with line tension γ, the stiffness of a real polar sine or cosine amplitude with integer angular harmonic m is Km​=πγ(m2−1)/R0​, when the enclosed area is fixed. The equipartition theorem gives ⟨um2​⟩=kB​TR0​/[πγ(m2−1)] for m≥2. A positive-frequency complex Fourier mode coefficient has half this variance. The uniform mode is forbidden and m=1 is translation.
Translation mode of a circular boundary (m=1)
Words: 55
Fixed-area capillary spectrum of a circular boundary OurBigBook.com
The first polar sine and cosine harmonics of a circular boundary represent displacements of its centre. A complete translation leaves perimeter and area unchanged, so line tension supplies zero stiffness to these modes. The centre of an unconfined domain has no normalizable positional thermal equilibrium in an infinite plane; recentering the boundary removes this freedom from a shape spectrum.

Lipid vesicle

Words: 167 Articles: 3
Lipid bilayer OurBigBook.com
A lipid vesicle is a closed lipid bilayer enclosing fluid. Its shape and thermal membrane undulations depend on membrane tension, membrane bending modulus, and constraints such as fixed enclosed volume.

Liposome

Words: 43
Lipid vesicle OurBigBook.com
A liposome is a closed artificial lipid vesicle enclosing an aqueous compartment. It may contain one lipid bilayer or several concentric bilayers. A single-bilayer spherical model distinguishes the inner aqueous radius, the boundary between opposing tail regions, and the outer head-group radius; finite molecular packing constrains all three.

Fixed-volume capillary spectrum of a cylindrical membrane (⟨uq2​⟩)

Words: 57
Lipid vesicle OurBigBook.com
For a tension-dominated cylindrical lipid vesicle of fixed length L and volume, a real axisymmetric sine amplitude uq​ has stiffness Kq​=πσL[(qR0​)2−1]/R0​. Fixed volume requires a mean-radius shift −uq2​/(4R0​). Stable modes have ⟨uq2​⟩=kB​T/Kq​ by the equipartition theorem. Modes with qR0​<1 have the Rayleigh–Plateau instability, rather than a negative equilibrium variance. Bending modifies very short wavelengths and near-marginal modes.

Words: 45
Lipid vesicle OurBigBook.com
An axisymmetric cylindrical membrane deformation is invariant under rotations about the cylinder axis, so its radius depends only on the axial coordinate. Its surface area is 2π∫R1+Rz2​​dz, and its enclosed volume is π∫R2dz. These scalar shape constraints are the basis of the fixed-volume capillary spectrum of a cylindrical membrane.

The Hamaker constant sets the strength of pairwise-summed van der Waals attraction between macroscopic bodies across a medium.

For fully dissociated electrolytes at the same temperature and solvent permittivity, linear screening theory gives λD−2​∝∑i​ci​zi2​=2I. A divalent symmetric salt of formula concentration c has I=4c, not c or 2c. ion association and nonideal concentrated-solution effects limit this comparison.

Helfrich repulsion is the entropic interaction produced when neighboring membranes suppress each other's thermal undulations. Its free energy per area scales as (kB​T)2/(kc​d2).

A membrane unbinding transition sends the equilibrium layer spacing to infinity. In a dilute lamellar stack, competition between a quadratic virial attraction and cubic Helfrich repulsion gives a continuous transition with spacing exponent one.

The Helfrich energy of a fluid membrane combines surface tension with curvature elasticity. Without spontaneous curvature or a topological term,
E=∫dS[σ+2kc​​(2H)2].

Spherical-particle wrapping by a fluid membrane (E/(πκ)=(4−2wˉ)ξ+σˉξ2)

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Helfrich energy OurBigBook.com
In a bound-cap model, an adhered sphere of radius r covers area A=2πr2ξ with ξ=1−cosα∈[0,2]. Its excess area over its circular footprint is πr2ξ2. The Helfrich energy of that spherical cap is 4πκξ, adhesion gives −wA, and membrane tension gives σπr2ξ2. Setting wˉ=wr2/κ and σˉ=σr2/κ yields the displayed expression. Free-surface deformation, neck structure, Gaussian curvature and topology changes are omitted. Full wrapping alone does not prove scission.
Tension-dependent wrapping phase diagram (ξ∗​=[(wˉ−2)/σˉ][0,2]​)
Words: 75
Spherical-particle wrapping by a fluid membrane OurBigBook.com
For positive membrane tension, the bound-cap energy is convex in indentation. Its constrained minimum is the unconstrained value (wˉ−2)/σˉ clipped to [0,2]. No wrapping occurs at wˉ≤2, partial wrapping at 2<wˉ<2+2σˉ, and full wrapping at wˉ≥2+2σˉ. At zero tension the expression is linear, with all indentations degenerate at wˉ=2. These phase boundaries belong to the specified cap model and can move when free-membrane and neck energies are included.

Fluid membrane shear response

Words: 42
Helfrich energy OurBigBook.com
A fluid surface has no equilibrium static in-plane shear modulus, because material can rearrange after shear. This does not set its membrane tension or membrane bending modulus to zero. Time-dependent deformation can also produce viscous in-plane shear stress; absence of a static elastic coefficient is not absence of dissipation.

Thermal membrane undulation

Words: 275 Articles: 3
Helfrich energy OurBigBook.com
A thermal membrane undulation is a shape fluctuation excited by thermal energy. In a planar membrane, a Fourier mode has stiffness kc​q4+σq2, so tension suppresses long-wavelength excess area while bending suppresses short wavelengths.
Micropipette aspiration
Words: 90
Thermal membrane undulation OurBigBook.com
In a membrane-mechanics experiment, a narrow glass pipette applies a controlled pressure difference and draws a tongue of membrane into its opening. Imaging the aspirated length and vesicle geometry estimates the change in apparent membrane area. At low tension, much of that change can flatten thermal undulations; at higher tension it can measure actual area dilation. For ideal spherical caps with pipette radius Rp​ and vesicle radius Rv​>Rp​, the Young–Laplace equation gives Δp=2σ(1/Rp​−1/Rv​). Bending at the rim, adhesion and a membrane-associated cytoskeleton can require corrections to this simple geometric inference.
Membrane bending rigidity (κ)
Words: 65
Thermal membrane undulation OurBigBook.com
This coefficient multiplies the squared mean-curvature term 2κ​∫(2H−C0​)2dA in the Helfrich membrane energy. It has units of energy, unlike a beam's flexural rigidity. For small height modes of a nearly flat membrane of area A, with Fourier normalization hq​=A−1∫h(x)e−iq⋅xd2x, quadratic bending and tension energies give ⟨∣hq​∣2⟩=kB​T/[A(κq4+σq2)] by the equipartition theorem. Thermal-flicker measurements can therefore separate short-wavelength bending from longer-wavelength tension effects.
Membrane fluctuation spectrum under tension (⟨∣hq​∣2⟩=kB​T/[A(σq2+κq4)])
Words: 85
Thermal membrane undulation OurBigBook.com
For small-slope height fluctuations of a nearly planar membrane, A is projected area, σ is membrane tension, κ is membrane bending modulus, and q is a wavenumber. With a Fourier convention in which the mode amplitude hq​ has units of length, the quadratic Helfrich membrane energy and the equipartition theorem give the displayed thermal variance. Bending dominates for q≫σ/κ​, giving a q−4 spectrum. Tension dominates at smaller q, giving q−2. The corresponding membrane elastic length is κ/σ​ when length is measured as 1/q; a wavelength convention multiplies it by 2π.

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Small-slope elastic membrane energy OurBigBook.com
For a tension-dominated membrane with internal dimension D, the massless Gaussian height covariance has spectrum kB​T/(σq2). Removing the uniform translation mode leaves the height difference well-defined. Its variance grows linearly with distance for D=1, logarithmically for D=2, and approaches a cutoff-dependent constant for D>2. A microscopic cutoff is necessary when the short-distance integral diverges. This distinguishes rough positional order from a failure of the local small-slope approximation.

Adding positive quadratic confinement t∫h2/2 to the membrane energy changes its height spectrum to kB​T/(σq2+t). The continuous height-shift symmetry is explicitly broken. Connected correlation function decay on the finite length ξ and the height-difference variance saturates for every internal dimension, although its saturation value can depend on a microscopic cutoff.
